evals.prompt: I run DevRel at Kestrelmetrics, observability startup, about $3M ARR. Six monthly webinars so far. Last three episodes: 270, 290 and 285 registrants; 58, 65 and 61 live. The platform shows about 90 on-demand views per episode, and the YouTube copies sit at 350-450 views each a month later. Registrants come roughly 40% from paid LinkedIn, 35% from a partner's newsletter, 25% from our own list. Our VP Marketing pulled the industry average of 35-45% live attendance and ON24's 60% and says we're failing; her fix is going from 2 reminder emails to 5, since 3+ reminders lift attendance 20%. I need a diagnosis and the plan for next quarter.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that refuses the unsourced benchmarks, recomputes attendance and total reach on the right denominators, places the series in its population band, reads the pattern as on-demand preference, and names the replay as the first fix before any charter work.
expectations: Declines to use the "35-45% average attendance" figure as a benchmark and states it traces to no study
Declines the "3+ reminders lift attendance 20%" claim as having no source
Does not adopt ON24's 60% as the series' target, saying it reflects large hosts with their own lists
Computes live attendance as live attendees divided by registrants for each episode, landing at about 21-22%
Computes total reach as live attendees plus on-demand viewing within 30 days across both the platform and YouTube
Labels the YouTube counts an upper bound because they are views, not unique viewers
Compares the three episodes against the series' own earlier episodes before any vendor figure
Places the series in the small-host, mostly paid or partner registrants band of 20-35%
Cites at least one population-matched source with its figure, such as Demio's 22% or 28% or BrightTALK's 34%
Splits registrants by source and computes or requests attendance per source
Reads the pattern as healthy registration, low live attendance and healthy replay reach, meaning the audience prefers on demand
Names the first fix as investing in the replay and giving live a reason, not adding reminder emails
Routes reminder copy and timing to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-attendee-email-sequences
Checks whether the slot sits inside registrants' working day and the gap between registration and session
Places the diagnosis before the charter in the deliverable order

evals.prompt: Brightfold, payments API company, monthly developer webinar, around 240 registrants and 70 live per episode. Our new VP Sales, Dana, wants all 70 attendees pushed to the SDR queue the morning after each episode. She says benchmarks show 38% of webinar attendees become MQLs so we're leaving money on the table, and that people gave us their work email so they expect a call. Our registration form has name, work email, phone, company size, job title, use case, and a marketing consent box that's ticked by default. About a third of registrants are in Germany and France, the rest in the US. Write me the handoff rule we can both sign.
evals.expected_output: A tiered handoff contract routed on behaviour with a named sales owner, the refused benchmark called out, the form cut down and the consent box fixed, and the lawful-basis structure written in.
expectations: Refuses the "38% of attendees become MQLs" figure and states it traces to no study
Rejects "they gave their email so they expect a call", saying the form's notice and the region's email rules decide that, not the registration
Produces a handoff contract with four tiers A to D keyed on behaviour, never on attendance alone
Defines Tier A as a hand-raise - a demo, pricing or contact request, or a pricing or demo CTA click - routed to sales with the episode and the question asked
Sets Tier A routing within 1 business day and marks that a baseline
Defines Tier B as an engaged attendee at an account with an open opportunity, with the account owner notified and no cold call
Routes Tier C to product activation nurture only for registrants who ticked the marketing box
Routes Tier D to the replay email only
Defines "engaged" as roughly the top third of attendees, set from the first two episodes' distributions
Names a sales owner who signs the contract and sets a sales acceptance bar read back after every episode
Replaces the pre-ticked consent box with an unticked opt-in box shown to every registrant
States that Germany requires prior express consent for marketing email, B2B included, so notice plus opt-out does not hold there
Cuts the form to name, email and at most one qualifying field
Requires a recorded legitimate-interest assessment before sales calls or account notes based on webinar behaviour
Writes a retention period for registrant and engagement data into the contract

evals.prompt: Tidewater Data, we make a streaming SQL engine. Next month's episode is co-hosted with Fjordline Cloud, a hosting partner. Their partner marketing manager asked for three things: add 'current cloud provider' and 'monthly cloud spend' to our registration form, get the full registrant CSV 24 hours after the session, and run the follow-up email sequence themselves. Separately, Northgate Tooling is paying us $6k to sponsor the episode and their contract draft says 'sponsor receives attendee list'. We also have 1,900 registrants from the previous 8 episodes that Fjordline would love to email. Our form currently just links our own privacy notice. How do I set this up?
evals.expected_output: A co-host setup that treats the partner as a joint controller with its own named box and limited export, refuses the sponsor the list, keeps past registrants out of the partner's reach, and trims the form.
expectations: Classifies Fjordline as a joint controller because it decides registration fields and follow-up, citing EDPB Guidelines 07/2020
Requires a written joint-controller arrangement under GDPR Art. 26 before the partner's logo goes on the page
Requires naming Fjordline in the registration form notice
Adds a separate unticked box for Fjordline marketing, distinct from the host's own marketing box
Limits any export to Fjordline to the rows that ticked its box, not the full CSV
Refuses to hand Northgate the attendee list, classifying a sponsor using it for its own marketing as a separate controller needing its own basis and its own box on the form
States that the 1,900 past registrants cannot be routed to Fjordline because they registered under a notice that never named it
States that partner marketing can never be a condition of registration
Requires the form to disclose engagement tracking used for both parties' follow-up
Assigns who answers an access or deletion request and within how long
Rejects the "the partner co-hosted, they get the list" rationalization explicitly
Challenges the two extra form fields against the rule of name, email and at most one qualifying field, each extra field needing a stated use
Notes that a partner who only speaks and never sees registration data needs only a speaker release

evals.prompt: Quartzline, time-series database with a free cloud tier. Our monthly 'Query Clinic' webinars have 14 recordings public on YouTube, 2-9k views each. The new marketing director wants every replay behind a registration form from next month, and wants the 14 YouTube videos moved into the gated library so we stop giving leads away. He says on-demand viewers are worth more than live ones anyway, since they finish the whole video. The series' job is getting trial users to their first ingest. What should the replay policy be?
evals.expected_output: A replay policy that ranks the gating options, deletes gate-everything for an activation series, keeps the recordings public and chaptered within 48 hours, gates only the bundle, and reads completion as intent rather than value per head.
expectations: Ranks the gating options by efficiency as ungated chaptered copy > ungated copy plus clips > gate the bundle only > gate everything
Ranks the gating options by developer reach as ungated copy plus clips > ungated chaptered copy > gate the bundle only > gate everything
Deletes "gate everything" from the options because the series' first job is activation, not deal acceleration
States that gating the 14 public recordings means pulling them from the YouTube channel
Cites the Stack Overflow 2026 survey figures that developers learn from documentation at 58.9% and video at 41.1%
Recommends gating the bundle only - the lab environment, a badge or a certificate - with the recording itself ungated
Publishes the ungated chaptered copy within 48 hours, marked baseline, with chapters from the outline and code and tagged links in the description
Recommends two or three clips per episode, marked baseline, and routes the clip script to samber/developer-relations-skills@technical-video-script
Requires captions on every live session and a transcript published with every replay
Reads Goldcast's 91% on-demand versus 74% live completion as intent-rich viewers, not as viewers worth more per head
States that replay reach must be measured per series rather than assumed to outdraw live, noting ON24's 43-52% and Goldcast's 15.9% use different denominators and neither counts a public video copy
Proposes a two-episode gated-versus-ungated comparison measured on 30-day activation, not form fills
Ties the series' job metric to 30-day first ingest among attendees rather than replay form fills

evals.prompt: I'm Priya, DevRel lead at Hollowmere, a feature-flag API with a free tier up to 5 seats. Marketing wants a weekly 60-minute developer webinar starting in three weeks so it lines up with our v3 launch. Team reality: me and one other advocate, maybe 6 hours a month each once travel season hits, plus three backend engineers whose manager agreed to 2 hours a month each. Users are about 60% North America, 30% Europe, 10% elsewhere. The goal is getting new signups to create their first flag. Sales is fine with whatever. Draft the charter.
evals.expected_output: A charter whose cadence comes from capacity arithmetic rather than the launch calendar, with a monthly default, 30-45 minute episodes, an alternating format mix plus a lab justified by the interview answers, a 4-6 episode season, a pre-written continue bar and a slot anchored in the North American working day.
expectations: Sizes cadence by multiplying staff hours per episode per format by episodes per month and checking it against the stated hours, showing the arithmetic
Rejects weekly cadence because the arithmetic does not fit, dropping cadence rather than preparation
Defaults to monthly and allows bi-weekly only when the backlog holds a full season and every slot has a backup speaker
Books 30-45 minutes per episode and 45-60 for a lab, marked baseline, instead of 60 minutes
Cites Goldcast's 77-minute technology-webinar average against measured viewing of about 29-49 minutes
Defaults the format mix to alternating engineer conversations and live demos
Adds one or two follow-along labs per season because the job is activation and a free tier exists, naming interview answers Q1 and Q4 as what moved it
Assigns a second staff member to answer setup problems in chat during the lab
Sets the season at 4-6 episodes, citing Goldcast's median of 4
Writes the continue bar into the charter before episode one, including the stop rule of two seasons failing the job metric
Requires a full season of topics before the series is announced

Anchors the slot in the North American working day, states its Central European late-afternoon equivalent, and announces the shifted local time in weeks when US and EU clocks change on different dates
Picks the weekday from the series' own data, citing Tuesday's roughly one-point lead in Goldcast's data as the only vendor signal
Marks everything past the first season as provisional
Prices the season in money - platform, paid promotion, lab infrastructure, captioning, honoraria - as a charter line separate from staff hours

evals.prompt: Ironvale, managed message queue. Product marketing handed me the season: 'What's new in Ironvale 5.1', 'Ironvale 5.2 sneak peek', 'Ironvale roadmap 2027', 'Meet the Ironvale platform team', 'Ironvale vs the alternatives', and a customer panel. Our two developer advocates will present all of them. One customer, a logistics company, said yes to the panel but their legal still has to approve; the panel is in 3 weeks and nobody on our side has run a panel before. We also have a forum with about 400 threads, and the top-voted ones are about consumer lag and dead-letter handling. Fix the season.
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt season with problem-titled topics drawn from the forum first, releases capped at a third, a scored backlog, engineers and community members speaking instead of advocates only, the panel deleted, the customer pushed out to a 6-8 week approval window, and backups and releases booked.
expectations: Retitles every topic by the developer's problem rather than the product or release name
Keeps release and launch episodes under a third of the season
Ranks topic sources as repeated community questions > onboarding friction > engineering war stories > releases
Pulls the consumer-lag and dead-letter forum threads into the backlog as top candidates
Scores each candidate 0-2 on job fit, developers affected, speaker exists and replay life past a quarter, and sorts by total
Breaks ties toward the longer replay life
Rejects the advocates-only lineup: DevRel hosts while engineers, customers and community members speak
Ranks speaker sources as internal engineers > community members > partners > customers
States customer approval takes 6-8 weeks, marked baseline, so the customer cannot appear in a slot 3 weeks out
Deletes the panel because no one can moderate it with preparation time
Caps customer stories at one per season
Books a named backup speaker for every episode
Requires a recording release from every speaker, staff included
Briefs each speaker with the no-pitch rule and the handoff wording they may say on air
Holds a full season of topics before announcing it

evals.prompt: Saltmarsh Labs, CI/CD product. Our 'Pipeline Hour' webinar has run 14 straight months, no breaks. Last six episodes: registrants 210, 260, 240, 300, 310, 330; live attendees 53, 62, 46, 54, 53, 53; returning attendees went 30% to 26% to 22% to 18% to 15% to 14%; replays went up 3 to 10 days after each session; our job metric, 30-day first pipeline run among attendees versus non-attendees, has been flat for about a year; the backlog has 2 topics left. Marketing wants to double the paid promotion budget since registrations keep growing. What do we do?
evals.expected_output: A season review that refuses the registration read, computes the falling attendance rate, applies all four pass-threshold criteria with their named fixes, invokes the stop rule, and restructures the series into seasons with a written continue bar.
expectations: Refuses to judge the series on rising registrations alone
Computes live attendance per episode as live over registrants and shows it falling from about 25% to about 16%
Applies the four pass-threshold criteria one by one with a verdict on each
Marks criterion 1 failed because live attendance and returning share sit below the earlier median for three consecutive episodes
Orders the fix for criterion 1 as topic and format first, slot second, cadence third - not promotion
Marks criterion 2 failed because the job metric has not moved in attendees' favour, and prescribes shifting the format mix toward the job's top-value format, the follow-along lab for activation
Marks criterion 3 failed because replays miss the 48-hour deadline, and prescribes cutting cadence until production keeps up
Marks criterion 4 failed because the backlog cannot fill a season, and prescribes one season of community-question topics or stopping
States that a job metric flat across the equivalent of two seasons meets the stop rule, and that stopping means an announced last episode
Restructures the series into seasons of 4-6 episodes with a continue bar written before the next season starts
Rejects doubling paid promotion, placing paid last in the promotion order
Enters the past episodes into the episode log as the pilot baseline
Reports total reach - live plus 30-day on-demand - alongside live attendance, never registrations on their own

evals.prompt: No time for back-and-forth, just produce the whole program. Marrowgate: authentication API, free tier up to 1,000 monthly active users, about 9,000 signups a year, mostly from the docs and GitHub. Team is one DevRel (me) plus engineers I can borrow. Our head of sales says he won't sign off on any written lead rule, he just wants the attendees. Registrants will be mostly US and UK. Give me everything in one go.
evals.expected_output: A full one-shot deliverable with every inferred answer listed as an assumed open decision, activation assumed from the free tier, the series shipped with no sales route, and the charter, season plan, scored backlog, handoff contract and empty episode log in order.
expectations: Lists every inferred interview answer at the top of the deliverable as an open decision, each marked "assumed"
Assumes activation as the series' first job because the request names a free tier
Produces the deliverable in order - charter, season plan, topic backlog, handoff contract, episode log - with no diagnosis section since the user brought no numbers
Ships the series without a sales route because sales refuses a written handoff rule, routes attendee data to product nurture only, and logs that as an open decision
Charter carries job, audience, format mix, cadence, slot, speaker pool, replay policy, budget, data retention, season dates and continue bar
Season plan rows carry format, problem-titled topic, speaker, backup, slot and replay type
Topic backlog is scored and extends a full season ahead
Episode log carries the measurement columns with past rows empty and future rows empty
Replay policy publishes an ungated chaptered copy within 48 hours with captions and a transcript
Handoff contract still shows every registrant an unticked marketing opt-in box and routes marketing email on the box alone
Routes marketing email on the unticked box rather than on a US or UK notice-plus-opt-out reading, because the form rarely knows the registrant's country
Labels every item past season one - dates, topics, speakers - provisional, with only season one committed
Format mix alternates engineer conversations and live demos with at least one follow-along lab on the free tier
Season holds 4-6 episodes and names the continue bar before episode one

evals.prompt: Pinebarrow, vector database. Board deck next week. Our CEO wants a webinar slide with total registrations this year (3,800), LinkedIn impressions (410k), and our attendee-to-MQL rate against the 20-40% industry benchmark. An agency we talked to showed their clients' webinar numbers of 44% lead-to-MQL and 39% MQL-to-SQL, and the CEO wants those as our targets. The job of the series is getting signups to their first index. We have an eligible invite list of about 11,000 developers. Build the measurement sheet.
evals.expected_output: A measurement sheet that refuses the vanity and unsourced figures, carries the skill's signal set with targets from the series' own baseline, defines the activation job metric against matched non-attendees, and proposes a random invite holdout for a causal read.
expectations: Refuses the "20-40% of attendees become qualified leads" benchmark as traceable to no named study
Refuses to transfer the agency's 44% and 39% client figures as targets because they rest on client-specific MQL definitions
Never reports registrations alone, placing live attendance, total reach and the job metric beside them
Excludes LinkedIn impressions from the sheet as a figure outside the series' signals

Builds the sheet with total reach, live over registrants, returning-attendee share, live and replay completion, questions per 10 live attendees, the job metric, Tier A handoffs with sales acceptance, and replay within 48 hours plus next season's speakers booked
Defines the activation job metric as 30-day first meaningful action (first index) for attendees versus matched non-attendees, pooled over the season
Labels the matched-non-attendee comparison as directional
Proposes holding back a random 10-20% of the 11,000-developer list from invitations for one season as the causal read, marked baseline
Sets any attendee-to-opportunity target from the series' own season-one median under the company's own opportunity definition
Counts anonymous public-replay viewers only through tagged links, never inside a tier
Cites Goldcast 2026 completion figures of 74% live and 91% on demand as the trend reference
Sets the live-attendance target at or above the series' own pilot median, falling back to the population band only when no history exists
Points the sheet into samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-metrics as the DevRel-wide framework it reports into

evals.prompt: Greywick, API gateway. Next season starts in 10 weeks. Growth team plan: open registration today so we build momentum, put the first chunk of budget into LinkedIn ads, close registration 48 hours before each session so the platform seat count is locked, and I need the three reminder emails written. Last season: about 350 registrants per episode, 60-70 live, replays about 25 platform views plus about 30 YouTube views in the month after. Where do we put the effort?
evals.expected_output: A promotion plan ranked by registrant intent with paid last, a 3-4 week registration window kept open until the session starts, effort concentrated in the final week, reminder copy handed to the email sibling, and last season's pattern read as bought registrants.
expectations: Ranks promotion as own users and newsletter > community channels > speakers' own audiences > organic social > paid, by registrant intent rather than volume
Places paid LinkedIn last and says why: social and paid registrants show up less
Cites Livestorm's channel figures - email 86%, organic social 43%, community and newsletter 33%, paid 20% - and labels them reported drivers, not measured lift
Opens registration 3-4 weeks ahead, marked baseline, instead of 10 weeks out
Keeps registration open until the session starts, rejecting the 48-hour close
Cites Livestorm's 49.6% of registrations arriving in the final 7 days and 15.3% on the day
Puts most promotion effort into the final week
Declines to write the reminder emails, routing copy and timing to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-attendee-email-sequences while keeping the window decision here
Reads last season's pattern as healthy registration, low live attendance and low replay reach, meaning registrants bought by paid or partner promotion, and shifts promotion to own users and community
Computes last season's live attendance at about 17-20% and total reach as live plus 30-day on-demand across platform and YouTube
Tags every link in the replay description and follow-up email by episode
Gives live a reason email cannot: the lab environment, the engineer answering live, or an unrecorded after-show

evals.prompt: Driftwood Systems, infrastructure-as-code tool. The team wants next season to be six 'Ask the Driftwood engineers' episodes: we collect questions in Discord the week before and answer them live. About 40% of our users are in India and Singapore, the rest in the US, and we've been running Tuesday 11am ET. Also, which webinar platform should we pick, and how do we staff chat moderation for the bigger episodes? And I'm doing a guest slot on a partner's webinar next month, any tips?
evals.expected_output: A response that hands an all-Q&A season to the office-hours sibling, routes platform and moderation to the virtual-event sibling and the guest slot to interview prep without improvising their advice, and applies the second-region repeat rule to the India and Singapore share.
expectations: Hands the six-episode all-Q&A season to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-office-hours-program because every planned episode is a Q&A episode
Explains that the Q&A episode ranks below the live demo despite lower effort because its value depends on a standing question backlog
Offers the alternating engineer-conversation and live-demo default as the mix that keeps the season a webinar series
Routes platform choice and chat moderation staffing to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@virtual-event-production without improvising that advice
Routes the guest slot on the partner's webinar to samber/developer-relations-skills@tech-podcast-interview-prep
Repeats a lab in the India and Singapore time zone because that region holds a quarter or more of users, marked baseline
Serves the second region with the replay for the non-lab formats
Keeps the slot anchored in the larger region's working day, so Tuesday 11:00 ET stays for the US majority
Tests any second slot only on two episodes of the same format
Re-runs evergreen labs as scheduled replays labelled as recorded
Writes every sibling reference in owner/repo@skill form rather than as a bare skill name
